content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated guidelines for tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment, particularly for children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of individuals with TB. These guidelines provide several treatment options tailored for countries with high or upper-middle income and low TB incidence. A systematic review has shown that a 3-month regimen of daily rifampicin plus isoniazid (3RH) is as effective as longer regimens of daily isoniazid monotherapy (6H or 9H). The 3RH regimen is recommended as an alternative to 6H or 9H for children and adolescents under 15 years of age in high TB incidence settings. This recommendation is based on its shorter duration, higher treatment completion rates, and safer profile. The main outcomes considered in the evaluation of these regimens include the incidence of active TB, mortality, adverse events, treatment completion rates, and the emergence of drug-resistant TB. In high TB incidence countries, where the estimated TB incidence rate is ≥100 per 100,000 population, shorter regimens like 3RH are seen as more feasible and scalable due to their reduced resource requirements and fewer clinic visits. A systematic review of one randomized controlled trial (RCT) and two observational studies found no cases of clinical TB disease in the RCT. Children receiving 3RH or 4RH (3 or 4 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid) had fewer radiographic abnormalities suggestive of TB, higher adherence rates, and fewer adverse events compared to those on 9H. The evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of 3RH is considered low quality, but the benefits outweigh the harms, as agreed upon by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The GDG emphasized the importance of using pediatric fixed-dose combinations of rifampicin and isoniazid to improve acceptability and feasibility. However, caution is advised when prescribing 3RH to people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) due to potential drug-drug interactions, particularly with protease inhibitors or nevirapine. Surveillance systems for rifampicin-resistant TB are also critical to monitor the emergence of resistance. The cost-effectiveness of 3RH is favorable due to its shorter duration, higher completion rates, and safer profile, which require fewer resources compared to longer regimens. Although direct evidence on cost-effectiveness in children is limited, data from adult populations support the use of shorter preventive treatment regimens, including 3RH. The GDG strongly recommends 3RH as a preventive treatment option for children and adolescents under 15 years of age in high TB incidence countries. This recommendation is based on its shorter duration, higher completion rates, and availability of child-friendly formulations, despite the low quality of evidence. Further research is needed to develop reliable methods for excluding active TB in children and to address gaps in data on drug resistance and cost-effectiveness.
